meta.title: Who really said "Thank You for the Gift Book. I Shall Lose No Time In Reading It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No letter of Disraeli's has ever been produced containing it. The quip is a floating Victorian joke, printed in 1871 crediting only an unnamed botanist, and pinned on him from 1898.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thank You for the Gift Book. I Shall Lose No Time In Reading It'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Disraeli. First printed in 1871 crediting an unnamed "celebrated botanist", the joke was later fathered on Gladstone, Thackeray, Holmes and Disraeli.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Disraeli — an anonymous Victorian joke
answer.authorDates: First printed 1871 · credited to no one by name
answer.sourceLine: The quip was already circulating in 1871, when The British Quarterly Review credited it to an unnamed “celebrated botanist” in an essay on letter-writing. Disraeli’s name was attached to it only in 1898, seventeen years after his death, and his own biographer Wilfrid Meynell printed it in 1903 while conceding the evidence for it was thin and offering no source.

source.excerpt: A celebrated botanist used to return thanks somewhat in the following form:—‘I have received your book, and shall lose no time in reading it.’ The unfortunate author might put his own construction on this rather ambiguous language.
source.trailTitle: How an anonymous joke became a Disraeli quote
trail: 1871 — the joke, with no owner. An essay on letters and letter-writing in The British Quarterly Review attributes the formula to “a celebrated botanist” and leaves him unnamed. This is the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator. Read the volume ↗

1898 — Disraeli’s name arrives. Quote Investigator documents a New York Times piece of 9 July 1898 saying Lord Beaconsfield had “a kind of stereotyped form of acknowledgment” to the effect that he “would lose no time in reading them.” That is twenty-seven years after the first printing and seventeen years after Disraeli’s death in 1881. Quote Investigator ↗

1903 — his biographer prints it, and hedges. Wilfrid Meynell’s Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography gives it on page 135 as a reply “to an author, presenting an impossible book,” then judges that the ambiguity “fathered upon Disraeli, might very well be his” while allowing that there is “as little evidence of the paternity as that which sometimes satisfies a magistrate of sentiment” — an endorsement resting on thin evidence, not a source. See page 135 ↗

Today — still unsourced. Wikiquote keeps the line in the Unsourced list on its Disraeli talk page, citing Meynell’s “it might very well be his” and noting the same quip has been fathered on Heinrich Heine, George Bernard Shaw and Winston Churchill. Wikiquote ↗
source.excerptNote: The 1871 printing arrives already anonymous — the joke is presented as a habit of an unnamed man, not as a remark anyone can date or verify.

source.rightsNote: Both documented printings are long out of copyright: The British Quarterly Review of 1871 and Wilfrid Meynell’s Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography of 1903 were published well before 1931 and are public domain in the United States. The sentence itself is anonymous, so no author or estate has ever held a claim to it.

author.name: Benjamin Disraeli
author.kicker: The man the joke was pinned on
author.heading: Why it stuck to Disraeli
author.metaLine: 1804–1881 · British Prime Minister, novelist & 1st Earl of Beaconsfield
author.bio: Benjamin Disraeli (21 December 1804 – 19 April 1881) was a British statesman and novelist who served twice as Prime Minister — briefly in 1868, then from 1874 to 1880 — and was made 1st Earl of Beaconsfield in 1876. He was a working author as well as a politician, which made him a plausible magnet for any joke about being sent unwanted books by hopeful writers. That plausibility is exactly why the line stuck to him: it sounds like Disraeli, but no letter or manuscript in his hand has ever been produced containing it.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: Over roughly 140 years the same two-line joke has been handed to at least seven named people, none of whom left a letter containing it. Quote Investigator’s chronology dates each handover.

items.why: The New York Times gave it to Lord Beaconsfield in 1898, and Wilfrid Meynell put it in his 1903 biography under “Of Men and Books” — where he judged that the ambiguity “fathered upon Disraeli, might very well be his,” while allowing in the same breath that there is “as little evidence of the paternity as that which sometimes satisfies a magistrate of sentiment.” An endorsement resting on thin evidence, not a source. Meynell, page 135 ↗

A New Zealand paper ran it as Gladstone’s acknowledgment a year before the Times gave it to Disraeli — the joke was simply being fitted to whichever statesman was in the reader’s mind. Quote Investigator ↗

The earliest attachment to a specific person that Quote Investigator found is in Rhoda Broughton’s 1894 novel A Beginner, where it is recalled as the bishop’s “masterly acknowledgment of a presentation copy.” A novel is not evidence. Quote Investigator ↗

items.who: Thomas Bailey Aldrich and Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
items.why: Newspapers gave the same anecdote to the poet-editor Aldrich in 1900 — there an ambitious young author and a volume of forbidding length — and to “Dr. Holmes” in 1902, where it is a self-satisfied author sending a complimentary copy. Quote Investigator ↗
A Massachusetts newspaper column handed the joke to Thackeray in 1931, half a century after Disraeli’s death and sixty years after its first known printing. Quote Investigator ↗

The variant “Thank you for sending me a copy of your book. I’ll waste no time reading it” was printed in a 1982 quotation collection and credited to the classical scholar Moses Hadas “in a letter” — no such letter has been produced. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest instance located by Quote Investigator, in 1871, credits nobody by name — just “a celebrated botanist” — and QI reports it has seen no direct evidence, meaning no letter from any prominent individual containing the joke. Its hypothesis is that the phrase was rarely actually sent, and lived mainly in comic anecdotes. Read the full chronology ↗

context.heading: A joke that kept changing owners
lead: The line works because it is a trap dressed as a courtesy. “I shall lose no time in reading it” can mean I will start at once or I will not spend a second on it, and the author holding the letter has no way to tell which. Victorian periodicals loved it precisely for that: it was a printable way to be rude in public.

That is also why it has no author. When The British Quarterly Review ran it in 1871 it belonged to “a celebrated botanist” whose name nobody bothered to give; by 1883 Nature was calling it a “well-known formula” and a travel writer called it “the old equivoque,” meaning it was already old furniture. A joke that generic needs a famous face, and over the next half-century it was fitted with several — Wilberforce, Gladstone, Disraeli, Aldrich, Holmes, Thackeray, and eventually the classicist Moses Hadas.
context.detailsSummary: How the joke travelled, in print
detailsBody: 1871 — The British Quarterly Review, in an essay on letters and letter-writing, gives it to “a celebrated botanist,” unnamed. This is the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗.

1883–1890 — Quote Investigator documents it as a stock joke rather than anyone’s remark: called “the old equivoque” in J. Fox Turner’s There and Back, a “well-known formula” in Nature, and finally listed in Punch’s “Dictionary of Phrases” in May 1890 with the gloss “No; not a single second.” See the citations ↗

1894 onward — the famous names arrive: Samuel Wilberforce (1894), Gladstone (1897), Disraeli (1898), Thomas Bailey Aldrich (1900), Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1902), Thackeray (1931), Moses Hadas (1982, in the “waste no time” wording). Collector Victor Steinbok’s antedating thread on the American Dialect Society list gathers several of the same finds. ADS-L, May 2010 ↗
context.pull: By 1883 it was already being called “the old equivoque” — a joke too well worn to belong to anyone.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article traces the quip to an 1871 British Quarterly Review printing crediting 'a celebrated botanist', lists attributions to Wilberforce (1894), Gladstone (1897), Disraeli/Lord Beaconsfield in the New York Times of 9 July 1898, Aldrich (1900), Holmes (1902), Meynell's hedged 1903 biography, Thackeray (1931) and Moses Hadas (1982), and concludes it has seen no direct evidence such as a letter from any prominent individual.
Project Gutenberg ebook 40223 is 'British Quarterly Review, American Edition, Vol. LIV — July and October, 1871'.

The text of that volume, in Art. V 'Letters and Letter Writing', contains: 'A celebrated botanist used to return thanks somewhat in the following form:--"I have received your book, and shall lose no time in reading it." The unfortunate author might put his own construction on this rather ambiguous language.'

Wilfrid Meynell, 'Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography', vol. 1 (1903), page 135, under the heading 'Of Men and Books', prints: 'To an author, presenting an impossible book: "Many thanks: I shall lose no time in reading it"' followed by 'This ambiguity, fathered upon Disraeli, might very well be his; and if there is as little evidence of the paternity as that which sometimes satisfies a magistrate of sentiment, we can say "Ben trovato" in all truth.'

Wikiquote's Talk:Benjamin Disraeli page lists 'Many thanks: I shall lose no time in reading it' in its Unsourced section, noting Meynell 'goes no further than to say "it might very well be his"' and that it has also been fathered on Heinrich Heine, George Bernard Shaw and Winston Churchill.

Benjamin Disraeli, 1st Earl of Beaconsfield, lived 21 December 1804 – 19 April 1881, was a British statesman, Conservative politician and writer, served twice as Prime Minister (1868 and 1874–1880) and was elevated to the peerage in 1876.

Victor Steinbok's May 2010 American Dialect Society (ADS-L) thread on this quotation documents the 1871 antedating, the 1883 'old equivoque' in J. Fox Turner's 'There and Back', a 1900 attribution to Thomas Bailey Aldrich in The Writer, and a December 1903 review of Meynell's Disraeli biography quoting 'Many thanks: I shall lose no time in reading it'.
The main Wikiquote article page for Benjamin Disraeli does NOT contain this quotation (checked so that no claim is attached to it).
